title: Lawsuit alleges Charlotte FC, Panthers parent company discriminate against men
content:
A former Charlotte FC executive and professional soccer player is suing the team’s owners, Tepper Sports & Entertainment, alleging that gender discrimination cost him his job.

The lawsuit, filed Thursday in the North Carolina Superior Court, argues that Dustin Swinehart, Charlotte FC’s former director of community engagement, was fired in 2024 after a colleague sent an email to a local family in the wake of a supervisory lapse at a youth camp the MLS team held. It claims Tepper Sports & Entertainment maintains separate standards for men and women, and that Swinehart was terminated despite a lack of discipline for more egregious conduct by female colleagues.

Swinehart, who played in the United Soccer League from 1996 to 2009 and is a member of the league’s Hall of Fame, alleges that his conflict with TSE Chief Human Resource Officer Kisha Smith developed after the incident at a youth camp in 2024. Before that, the two had few interactions, he said, as Smith was not part of his chain of command.

The situation started when twin boys walked off from the camp during the middle of the day; they were found unharmed. During a meeting about how to prevent similar incidents, Smith said the boys’ family should not receive any written communication from TSE. The lawsuit argues that Smith’s recommendation was beyond her purview and that TSE’s in-house counsel neither echoed nor endorsed it.

Swinehart’s direct boss approved his plan to refund the family’s camp payments and extend an offer for the family to attend a Charlotte FC game in a team suite. He then delegated that outreach to a member of the organization, who emailed the family. Swinehart says in his lawsuit that Smith called him and berated him about not following her recommendation. Smith, he claims, arranged for his firing soon after due to “insubordination.”

“I got fired for being kind, and I got fired for an email that I didn’t send,” Swinehart said Friday in an interview with The Athletic. “And that’s really tough. That’s really sad.”

A TSE spokesperson told The Athletic the organization is aware of the lawsuit but declined to comment as a matter of company policy regarding active litigation.

Swinehart’s lawsuit lays out alleged misconduct by female staffers, including intoxication on the job and the use of racist language, that he claims went unpunished. The disparity is framed as part of TSE’s public prioritization of elevating women into leadership roles, and the lawsuit argues Swinehart’s female replacement was unqualified to take over his role due to her lack of experience working in soccer.

“The evidence shows that had Plaintiff been female, he would not have been terminated. After all, he was the longest-tenured CFC employee and had amassed an exemplary employment record without a blemish. The incident for which he was terminated caused no harm to Defendant,” the lawsuit states. “Rather, his sole offense was to irk Defendant’s powerful CHRO because his direct report confirmed the family’s receipt of the refund and their interest in attending a match in a suite via email instead of a phone call.”

While Swinehart said he personally supports gender-diversity goals, he said TSE’s public desire to be a leader on the issue has left some male employees unsure where they stand and has contributed to turnover.

“I think specifically, to kind of the celebration of the advancement of women, it felt more presented as, ‘This is great. Look at all the things that are happening,'” Swinehart said. “But you could just start to notice, like, OK, so where does this leave me or where does this leave other employees with opportunities?”

Swinehart is seeking a jury trial and is requesting punitive damages and compensation for lost pay. His attorney, Josh Van Kampen, argues the firing violates Title VII of the Civil Rights Act and North Carolina state law.

Swinehart said he has struggled to find a comparable role since his dismissal and that an employment agent told him, “You have to find another job.” That’s contributed to personal stress, but he said he also hopes the lawsuit will help prevent similar situations and push TSE to improve as a workplace.

TSE, named for owner David Tepper, controls Charlotte FC, the NFL’s Carolina Panthers and Bank of America Stadium, where the teams play.

Charlotte FC is currently the No. 6 team in MLS’s Eastern Conference at 6-3-6. The team will resume play after the World Cup break Wednesday against Atlanta United.

Joseph Person contributed to this report.
